unit.title: Your trading plan
unit.description: Write your plan, keep a journal, ride out the streaks and make the leap sensibly

texts: Rule or wish?
A plan says how much time you put in, what you trade, when you enter, where the stop goes, how much you risk, how you exit and when you stop. Do these sentences work?
Concrete rule
Vague phrase
I enter if it bounces off the 50-session average with a reversal candle and above-average volume
It can be checked: two people reading it would do the same thing.
I enter when it looks clear
What's «clear»? It'll mean something different every day.
Stop below the low of the reversal candle, at least 1.5 ATR away
It says exactly where the stop goes and why.
I get out when it feels like enough
The emotion of the moment will decide, not the plan.
If it hasn't reached 1R within 15 sessions, I get out
A time-based exit, measurable and not up for debate.
Sort the five sentences.
A concrete rule can be checked: **two people reading it would do the same thing**. If it isn't written like that, it isn't a plan: it's a hunch.
Hint: could you check afterwards whether you followed it?
Rule or wish? Sort each sentence
Up 8 % in an hour
Pablo
My plan says: I only enter on a reversal candle at a support.
A share shoots up 8 % in an hour. It doesn't meet any of his rules.
It's getting away from me! Do I get in?
What do you tell Pablo?
Get in: it's a once-in-a-lifetime chance
That's FOMO. And if it goes wrong, he won't know whether his plan works.
Don't get in, and log it in your journal as a temptation
That's it! There'll be plenty of chances. A plan only works if you follow it.
Get in with a little, just in case
A little or a lot, it's still breaking the plan.
Write the plan when you're calm. You'll need it when you're not.

steps.title: Limits protect you from yourself
steps.body:
«I don't trade on earnings day. I don't average down. I don't move the stop against me. If I lose 6 % in a month, I stop until the next month. If the account falls 15 % from its peak, I halve my risk and review the plan.»

And every 20 trades, a review of the stats.
steps.key: If it isn't written down, it isn't a plan: it's a hunch.
steps.tip: Size of each trade: 1 % risk or less while you're learning.

texts: What Marta's journal said
Marta
I've got 40 trades logged in my journal.
The ones that followed the plan: **+0.3R** on average. The ones where I broke it: **−0.6R**.
What should Marta change?
Her system: it doesn't work
When she follows it, she wins. Changing it would throw away what works.
Stop breaking the plan
Exactly! The problem is the exceptions. That's where she can improve.
Drop the journal, it stresses her out
Without the journal, she'd never have found out.
My memory told me the exceptions were my best trades…
Your memory keeps the wins and forgets the mistakes. The journal doesn't.
Go through your journal
On each line of the journal you note the reason, the entry, the stop, the size, the result in R and how you felt. Did you follow the plan?
Followed the plan
Broke the plan
I entered at the support on a reversal candle, as the plan says
Entry reason as per the plan: that way you can measure whether the system works.
I rushed in: «it was getting away from me»
Rushing in is the fingerprint of FOMO. Note down the emotion.
I moved the stop against me «to give it room»
Moving the stop against you turns a small loss into a big one.
I sold half at 2R, as the plan said
The exit was decided before getting in.
I doubled my size after two losses
Size is always the same, win or lose.
Check the five trades.
Comparing trades **inside and outside the plan** is usually the most revealing part of a journal: it tells you whether breaking the rules costs you money.
Hint: did the plan decide, or the emotion of the moment?
Inside or outside the plan? Check each line

steps.title: A journal entry
steps.body:
12/11, buy at €4.10, stop €3.95, target €4.40, 1R = €100, 666 shares. Result: +€180, +1.8R. Followed the plan: yes. Emotion: calm.

From this you get your win rate, average win and loss in R, **expectancy** and streaks.
steps.key: A journal turns your trades into data you can improve with.
steps.tip: Your journal shows you the mistakes your memory would rather forget.

texts: Ten losses in a row
Streaks are normal: with a 40 % win rate, almost half the time there are **8 or more losses in a row** in 100 trades. How much can your account take?
You risk 5 % per trade. After 10 losses in a row, how much is left of your €10,000?
About €9,500
About €6,000
Nothing: you lose it all
You're left with **€5,987**: each loss is 5 % of what's left. At 1 %, you'd have €9,044.
Find the risk at which, after 10 losses, you still have more than €9,000.
At **1 %**, 8 losses in a row are −7.7 %; at 5 %, −33.7 %. **Risk little so you can ride out the streaks.**
This way a bad streak won't knock you out of the game.
At this risk, a normal streak takes a big bite.
Lower the risk per trade
Seven losses in a row
Laura
I've got 120 trades in my journal, with positive expectancy.
And now I'm on **7 losses in a row**. My system doesn't work any more.
What should Laura do?
Switch systems
With a 40 % win rate, 7 in a row is the typical streak over 100 trades.
Stick to the plan and check she's applying the rules properly
Nice! If she hasn't broken any rules, she should let the statistics do their work.
Double the risk to win it back faster
If the streak goes on, the hole gets much deeper.
Winning 50 % of the time, the typical streak over 100 trades is **6** in a row.
If I switch after every bad streak, I'll never know if any of them worked.

steps.title: Drawdown
steps.body:
It's the fall in the account from its peak to the next low. Climbing back is harder than falling: after −15 % you need to gain **17.6 %**; after −35 %, almost **54 %**.

Rule in the example plan: if the account falls 10–15 % from its peak, you **halve your risk** and review.
steps.key: Streaks are just statistics: risk little so you can ride them out.
steps.tip: Eight misses in a row don't mean the plan is wrong: they mean you're on a losing streak.

u26l4.title: From the simulator to real money

texts: Talent or luck?
1,000 people trade **with no edge at all**: every trade is a coin toss. They start with 15 trades each.
Nobody has an edge. After 15 trades, will anyone look like a genius?
No: with no edge, nobody stands out
Yes: someone will have a spectacular result
They'll all end up the same
The luckiest one makes **€1,100**: 13 out of 15 right, tossing a coin.
Go up to 100 trades each and see how many lose.
With **15 trades**, luck looks a lot like talent. You need **50–100 logged trades**, and to look at expectancy after costs.
With more trades, luck evens out: close to half lose.
Look at the best one: looks like a genius, and was just lucky.
Increase each person's trades
12 out of 15
Raúl
I've won 12 of my first 15 trades!
I'm going to risk 10 % on each one. My system works.
What do you tell Raúl?
Go for it: the numbers speak for themselves
At 10 %, 6–8 losses in a row wipe out between half and two thirds of the account.
Stay at 1 % and log 50–100 trades
That's it! With a bigger sample and costs included, he'll know if he has an edge.
Move to real money right now, all in
Real money teaches you who you are. Start small.
Tweaking the system until the past looks perfect doesn't work either: that's **over-optimising**.
OK: more trades, same rules and small risk.

steps.title: The four phases
steps.body:
1. **Backtest:** 50–100 signals with their results.
2. **Out-of-sample:** other assets or another period, without changing the rules.
3. **Real-time simulator:** 2–3 months at least.
4. **Real money, bit by bit:** a fraction of your capital and half the risk.

If after 100 trades your expectancy after costs is negative or close to zero, you don't have an edge. It's not a failure: it's information.
steps.key: A system isn't proven until it works on new data and with enough trades.
steps.tip: The simulator teaches you to trade. Real money teaches you who you are. Start small.

s8boss.title: Final challenge: Risk, strategies and trading

u26l1-1.prompt: Put the parts of a trading plan in order.
u26l1-1.explanation: From the general (how much and what) to the specific (when I enter, how much I risk and how I exit).

u26l1-3.prompt: Monthly limit in the example plan: if I lose ____ in a month, I stop until the next month.
u26l1-3.explanation: A monthly cap cuts off revenge-trading spirals.

u26l1-5.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: That's a wish; a plan says when you enter, where the stop is and how much you risk
You don't need a plan if you've got intuition
u26l1-5.explanation: A plan is a set of testable rules, not good intentions.
feedback: That's the problem: it doesn't say when I enter, where the stop is or how much I risk.
OK… Entry at a support with a reversal candle, stop below the low, 1 % risk and exit at 2R. Better?
Intuition can't be reviewed or improved. A written plan can.

u26l1-6.prompt: Which things go in the «What I don't do» section of the example plan? Select all that apply.
options: I don't move the stop against me
I don't trade on earnings day
u26l1-6.explanation: Not setting a stop would mean skipping the foundation of the plan.

u26l1-7.prompt: Your plan caps total open risk at 5 % of the account and each trade risks 1 %. What's the maximum number of trades you can have open at once?

u26l1-10.prompt: Your plan says: «stop below the recent low». Apply it to this buy on a real chart.
u26l1-10.explanation: A specific rule applies the same way on any chart: the stop goes just below the recent low.

u26l1-11.prompt: How often does the example plan suggest reviewing the stats?
u26l1-11.explanation: A single trade tells you nothing; 20 start to show you something.

u26l2-1.prompt: Match each journal field with an example.
u26l2-1.explanation: Each field answers a question that will later help you improve.
right: No: I went in without a signal
Bounce off the 50 average with a hammer

u26l2-2.prompt: Match each journal statistic with what it tells you.
u26l2-2.explanation: No single statistic tells the whole story.
right: Whether the system makes money in the long run
Whether breaking the rules costs you money
How much you have to sit through

u26l2-3.prompt: Risk per trade: €100. You enter at €4.10 with the stop at €3.95. How many shares do you buy? (round down)

u26l2-4.prompt: Your journal has 20 trades: 8 winners and 12 losers. What's your win rate?

u26l2-5.prompt: In those 20 trades, the winners made +2R on average and the losers −1R. What's your expectancy per trade?

u26l2-6.prompt: Which journal statistic tells you whether your system makes money in the long run?
u26l2-6.explanation: It combines your win rate with your average win and loss.

u26l2-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Without a journal you can't work out your expectancy or see your mistakes
u26l2-10.explanation: What you don't measure, you can't improve.
feedback: Then your journal would say you're a genius… and it would ruin you.
Your memory keeps the trade that went brilliantly and forgets the five small losses.
OK… If in 20 trades I find out I lose when I trade in a rush, it's worth it.
lines: Keeping a journal is such a drag 😩
Anyway, I can remember my trades.

u26l3-1.prompt: With a system that's right 50 % of the time, is it unusual to have 6 losses in a row in 100 trades?
options: It only happens with bad systems
u26l3-1.explanation: It's the typical longest streak in 100 trades.

u26l3-2.prompt: You risk 1 % per trade and take 8 losses in a row. How much does your account fall? (round to one decimal place)

u26l3-4.prompt: Match the risk per trade with the fall after 8 losses in a row.
u26l3-4.explanation: Fall = 1 − (1 − risk)⁸. At 10 %, a normal streak takes more than half.

u26l3-5.prompt: Your account falls 15 % from its peak. How much do you need to gain to get back to it? (round to one decimal place)

u26l3-7.prompt: Bruno's account falls 15 % from its peak. What does the example plan say?
options: Halve the risk and review the plan
u26l3-7.explanation: When the account falls, you protect first; then you analyse.
feedback: It's the most common reaction and the most dangerous.
Without stops, the fall could be much bigger.
That way he protects his capital while he works out what's going on.

u26l3-10.prompt: The fall in the account from its peak to the next low is called ____.
u26l3-10.explanation: It's the measure that best reflects how much a strategy really hurts.

u26l4-1.prompt: Put the phases for validating a system in order.
u26l4-1.explanation: Each phase removes a type of self-deception before you risk money.

u26l4-5.prompt: Marta has passed the first three phases and is going to use real money. How does she start?
options: With all the capital she planned and the same risk as in the simulator
With double the risk to make up for lost time
With a small fraction of her capital and half the risk per trade
u26l4-5.explanation: The move to real money is made in small steps and only scaled up with data.
feedback: Real emotions are different: better to discover them with little money at stake.
There's no lost time: there's impatience, and impatience is a bad adviser.
Good: if her real stats look like the simulator's, she scales up bit by bit.

u26l4-6.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Better with a loan, so you make more
First more logged trades; then a small part and half the risk
u26l4-6.explanation: A good month on the simulator is a starting point, not proof.
feedback: With debt, a bad streak can be a serious problem.
OK: 100 trades in the journal, expectancy after costs and start small.
A month is very little… and with real money, fear and impatience change how I trade.
lines: I made 20 % on the simulator this month 🏆
Can I put my savings in now?

u26l4-7.prompt: Match each statistical trap with its description.
u26l4-7.explanation: They all make a system look better than it is.
right: Testing only on companies that still exist
Seeing a signal in the past as crystal clear when it wasn't in real time
Tweaking parameters until the past looks perfect

u26l4-9.prompt: You're going to start with €2,000 of real money and half your usual 1 % risk. How much do you risk per trade?

u26l4-10.prompt: First «small» trade: your account is €2,000 and, since you're just starting, you risk 0.5 % at most. Choose the stop and amount.
u26l4-10.explanation: With half your usual risk, a bad streak when you start with real money won't take you out of the game while you check whether your stats look like the simulator's.

u26l4-11.prompt: What changes when you move from the simulator to real money? Select all that apply.
options: Your emotions when you see real losses
u26l4-11.explanation: The maths is the same; what changes is how you react, real costs and the taxman.
